title: It Takes Listening to Each Other
author: Ogden Valley City District 3 Council Member Kay Hoogland
paragraphs: I took a risk on November 5. I invited both residents and developers to our District 3 town hall to talk about construction traffic on Powder Mountain Road. Our community did not disappoint.

During my campaign last year, some folks criticized me for having dinner with a developer. While I don’t recall dining with a developer, I have had dinner with that developer’s mom, who was a neighbor and a fine lady.

But that criticism made me reflect. Is it productive to avoid talking to each other to solve problems? How can we find common ground, much less constructive solutions to our problems, if even breaking bread together is a valley sin? Our town hall demonstrated the importance of working together to solve community problems.

We didn’t dine with developers at the town hall. Yes, we had snacks and soft drinks. But we were there, together, for a lot of listening and learning about a valley problem: construction traffic and noise.

We all have a stake in the health and vibrancy of the valley and Ogden Valley City. We can’t retreat into isolated, hostile camps, whether developers, builders, residents, city name change supporters, traditional Ogden Valley namers, pioneer descendants, and new residents from California.

The first step in finding the common ground needed to solve community problems requires us to meeting and listen to each other. Creative and constructive solutions require participation of all sides of a given issue.

The city cannot stop truck traffic on Powder Mountain Road. It is a UDOT highway, not a city road. Construction truck road noise will never go away completely, as long as there is construction, be it next door or outside city boundaries. But we can at least find ways to lessen it through cooperation and problem-solving.

The principal developers and builders working in Wolf Creek and Powder Mountain sat at the front of the room. They were a little uncertain at first, not sure how the evening would go. By the same token, some of the residents who spoke were tentative and frustrated. But connections were made. People listened, and some solutions are being developed. The developers and builders briefly described their operations and plans, and steps they have taken to reduce traffic on Powder Mountain Road.

About 35 to 40 residents attended. For the most part, concerns were expressed respectfully. Some expressed themselves with force and emotion --  but most folks would if construction traffic woke them and their barking dogs at 4 a.m. The developer/builder guests were receptive to listening to the many residents who spoke. Residents were likewise respectful in listening to the remarks of the developer guests. Yes, there was skepticism on the faces of some. But there was also earnest listening to the developers’ updates:

Powder Mountain: The resort intentionally centered much of its processing on site, including gravel production and soil processing. This has reduced the truck traffic that would be needed, although building materials still require transport up Powder Mountain Road. Brandi Hammon, Powder Mountain CEO, supported the idea of having a hotline or other mechanism where residents can report specific bad actors or extreme noise incidents.

Michael Brenny: Mike’s organization is building condos and townhomes near the entrance to Powder Mountain. His chief of construction tries to inspect subcontractors’ trucks to make sure they are in good order. Brenny keeps the soil he can at the top of the mountain but has to truck off soil that has too much rock to be processed economically at the Powder Mountain processing site.

Eden Valley Opportunities/Lewis Homes: Jeff Scadden, operations director, explained how they produced gravel on site at Cobabe Ranch, and earlier at the Bridges. Yes, it is noisy and dusty, but it is more economical and keeps traffic out of the canyon and off valley roads. Their building activity is expected to significantly drop this fall as water rights remain in litigation.

I heard from residents that they thought more could be done. But showing up and listening for 90 minutes to residents’ concerns is a key step for our developers and builders to help address the concerns we share.

Truck screening: Our newly appointed Public Works Manager, Glenn Gammell, shared a big idea after the meeting wrapped up. We can ask the Utah Highway Patrol’s truck inspection group to stop and inspect trucks on Powder Mountain Road for proper mufflers and other equipment that restricts noise. Old trucks and ineffective or absent mufflers are leading causes of highway noise.

Engineering: Our city engineers at J-U-B Engineering are pursuing other solutions, such as limiting road weight, better signage, designating specific truck routes, and other measures to reduce resident disruption described more fully in another article in this issue.

Construction rules: The city council is considering a new, stricter ordinance driven by Council Members Peggy Dooling-Baker and Don Hickman to address construction noise and other negative side effects of building.

A reporting site: Residents and developers both asked for a hotline or website to report specific incidents. Builders can act on specifics if they have a contractor name, license plate, or other vehicle descriptions.

Construction disruption has no perfect solution. However, we can work together to lessen the extreme impacts that residents are experiencing. I’m grateful to the residents who showed up to voice their concerns and to the builders and developers who showed up to listen and consider what we can do together to address these challenges.
